accuracy.evidence: Checked against US Common Core K.MD.B.3 (classify objects into given categories), Development Matters 2021 for 3-4 year olds (compare objects by size, talk about shapes using informal and mathematical language) and NCETM early-years guidance on sorting by one attribute. Attribute, criterion and the idea that one set can be sorted several ways are stated correctly; the six lab toys are coded so every rule gives one clean answer.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets documented early-sorting slips: switching rule halfway (a small red toy dropped among big reds gets 'It looks like the ones in there, but we sort by size now'), believing a set can only be sorted one way (prediction 1), and treating a big circle and a small circle as different kinds (prediction 2). The guess-my-rule step answers a wrong guess by naming a hoop where that attribute is mixed.

lab_distinct.evidence: flagsort keeps one fixed set of six toys coded by colour, size and shape and re-sorts that same set under three rules, then reverses the task (find the misfit, infer the rule). flagmatch pairs identical items and flagshape names shape properties; neither changes the rule on a fixed set. The shingle gate passed.

lab_teaches.evidence: The child sorts the same six toys three times and sees the hoop contents change with the rule, which is the discovery that one set has many sortings; the done messages only confirm it ('Same toys, new rule, new groups'). Finding the misfit and inferring the rule make the child check every toy against one attribute.

predictions.evidence: Two locked predictions with tempting wrong options: 'No, only by colour' before re-sorting the same toys by size, and 'No, they look too different' for a big red circle and a small blue circle before the shape sort puts them in one hoop. Each is tested by the task straight after and the done message quotes the child's guess.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Five rotating questions with tagged wrong answers: grouped by kind instead of colour, put all three together, used colour when the rule is size, said Mia had no rule, put a square in the circle hoop because of its colour, and thought new toys are needed for a new rule. Each tag gets its own one-line correction.

readability.evidence: Kid text scores FK -0.7 against the family limit of 5.0 with short sentences such as 'Put all the red ones here.' Adult text scores FK 7.9 against 10 while using the precise terms attribute, criterion, classify and sort, plus the standard code K.MD.B.3.

no_filler.evidence: The filler gate passed. Every kid paragraph gives an action to do with real toys and every adult paragraph carries curriculum, method, named mistakes or the lab outline; explanation overlap with every other lesson stays under the 12 percent limit.

mobile.evidence: Screenshots at 360x640 in light and dark show the six toys in two rows of three above the hoops, toys big enough to drag with a thumb, two or three hoops filling the width with readable labels, and the Pick a toy / Into hoop buttons wrapping below the canvas. walk.cjs completed every Show me on desktop and iPhone 13.

accessibility.evidence: axe reported no WCAG 2.1 AA violations in either theme on desktop or iPhone and there were no console errors. Every drag has a button twin (Pick a toy, Into Red, the named toy buttons, Colour/Size/Shape), colour hoops also carry the colour word, and the canvas aria-label speaks each move, e.g. 'Picked: small blue square'.

sources: Common Core State Standards Mathematics K.MD.B.3
DfE (2021) Development Matters: mathematics, 3 and 4 year olds
NCETM Early Years: sorting and classifying by one attribute
